examples.state: Section 4 of 6, 8 bars. The dancers' energy drops for 8 bars before the biggest stretch of the routine.
examples.choice: breakdown: kick and bass out, pad and hats only, fill in bar 8
examples.reason: Removing the low end makes the following full section hit; keeping hats keeps the pulse for the dancers.

examples.state: Six sections over 72 bars at 124 BPM. Dancers start moving at once and peak in the final 16 bars.
examples.choice: short intro 4 bars, chorus returns three times, longest chorus last
examples.reason: Beat arrives early, the hook recurs, and the biggest block sits after the breakdown near the end.

examples.state: Section 2 of 5 leads into the first big group move. Should the build add layers or strip them?
examples.choice: build: low end out for 4 bars, filter rising, kick returns on downbeat
examples.reason: A stripped build followed by kick and bass on the downbeat is the standard way to make an arrival land.

examples.state: Chorus, phrase 3 of 4. Phrases 1 and 2 stated the 2-bar hook over the 4-chord loop unchanged.
examples.choice: repeat hook exactly; add octave doubling only
examples.reason: Exact repetition is normal; change one thing per 4-bar line, not the hook itself.

examples.state: Verse, 8 bars, groove-led funk at 108 BPM. Options: new chord each beat, two-bar riff vamp, or developing melody.
examples.choice: two-bar riff over a one-chord vamp
examples.reason: Funk and slower pop run on short riffs and static harmony; busy changes and developing lines sound like concert music.

examples.state: Last phrase of an 8-bar build before the drop. How should it end?
examples.choice: last bar: drop the bass, snare roll, cut on beat four
examples.reason: Vary only the last bar and leave a gap so kick and bass re-enter on the downbeat.

examples.state: Draft A repeats the hook with a new final note. Draft B replaces the hook with a longer rising melody over new chords.
examples.reason: B drifts into development; A keeps the hook and changes one detail.

examples.state: Draft plays continuous even eighth notes with no rests across 4 bars, chords changing every beat.
examples.reason: No space for the groove and too much harmonic motion; prefer rests, syncopation and one chord per bar or less.

examples.state: Chorus phrase identical to the previous phrase. The plan asks for no change at this block line.
examples.reason: Exact repetition is correct in loop music unless the plan calls for a change here.

examples.state: Verse at 120 BPM, dancers moving steadily, medium energy. Chorus next.
examples.choice: kick every beat, bass in eighths, closed hats in eighths, pad sidechained
examples.reason: Four-on-the-floor suits this tempo; save sixteenth hats and the lead hook for the chorus.

examples.state: Final chorus, highest energy of the piece, 16 bars.
examples.choice: all layers plus sixteenth hats, extra percussion, hook doubled up an octave
examples.reason: Raise intensity with density and layers rather than volume or tempo.

examples.state: Half-time section at 140 BPM, heavy floor work by the dancers.
examples.choice: sustained 808 on one note, clap on beat three, sparse kick
examples.reason: Half-time trap feel: long sub, one clap per bar, kick pattern carries the rhythm.

examples.state: A scene cut falls on bar 13, the first bar of a 4-bar block, inside an unbroken chorus.
examples.choice: crash on the downbeat plus a one-beat fill before it
examples.reason: The cut is on a block line, so mark it with a fill and crash without stopping the beat.

examples.state: A scene cut lands on beat three of bar 22, mid-phrase, small change of camera angle.
examples.choice: short stab on beat three; keep the groove
examples.reason: Mid-bar cuts get a small hit; save section changes for the next 4-bar line.

examples.state: Cut to a new location with a much bigger formation, starting at bar 33.
examples.choice: riser over bars 31-32, two-beat stop, full beat on bar 33
examples.reason: A big scene change earns a riser and a short stop with the full beat returning on the downbeat.

examples.state: Hook A: five notes, one bar, syncopated, repeated notes. Hook B: fourteen notes over four bars, wide range, even rhythm.
examples.reason: Short, rhythmic, narrow hooks loop and stick; B is a developing melody.

examples.state: Hook works over the first chord of the loop but clashes with the third chord.
examples.choice: reject; rework to fit every pass
examples.reason: A hook must repeat unchanged over the whole loop.

examples.state: Two 2-bar hooks: one starts on the downbeat with no rests, one anticipates beat one and leaves a beat of silence.
examples.choice: the anticipating hook with the rest
examples.reason: Syncopation and space give the dancers accents and leave room for an answer.
